title: Most Brits Oppose Tourist Taxes — Except in Hotspots
paragraphs: Many cities in Europe charge tourists a small tax when they stay overnight. Now, the UK government wants to let cities in England do the same. But according to a new survey, most British people do not like the idea, except in some popular tourist areas.

In September 2026, the government announced plans to let mayors in England charge a tourist tax on overnight stays. The tax is expected to be 5% per night on hotels, bed and breakfasts and other short-term rentals, and it will be called the "overnight visitor levy." The government hopes that the money will pay for local services, such as public transportation. However, some people in the hotel and restaurant industry worry that the tax could keep tourists away.

The survey was carried out online by the research company YouGov in September 2026. It asked 57,156 adults in Great Britain if they would support a small tourist tax. Overall, 51% said they would be against it, and 37% said they would support it.

However, the results were different in some places that are popular with tourists. For example, 67% of people in Edinburgh and Cambridge supported the tax. Support was also high in York, at 65%, Cornwall, at 61%, and Brighton and Hove, at 59%. In York, about one in every three pounds spent in the city is spent by tourists.
But not all tourist areas agreed. Most people in Somerset, the Isle of Wight and Devon were against the tax. In some seaside towns, such as Blackpool, only about 40% supported it.

Some places in the UK already have their own tourist taxes. In 2023, Manchester became the first city in the UK to charge visitors £1 per night. Edinburgh started charging a 5% tax in July 2026, and Wales plans to introduce a tax next spring.
